intro: Interviewers love look-alike pairs because a memorized definition does not survive them. For each pair, say the tell first: one sentence that separates the two. Then say when you would pick each.

pairs.tell: SQS is a queue one consumer group pulls from; SNS pushes each message to every subscriber.
pairs.pick_a: Buffer work so a worker fleet can process it at its own pace, with retries and a dead-letter queue.
pairs.pick_b: Fan one event out to many destinations at once: email, Lambda, or several SQS queues.

pairs.tell: SQS deletes a message once it is processed; Kinesis keeps an ordered, replayable log that many consumers read independently.
pairs.pick_a: Independent tasks where order does not matter (or FIFO per group) and each message is handled once.
pairs.pick_b: Clickstreams or telemetry where several consumers need the same ordered records and you may replay them.

pairs.tell: SNS is fast, simple fan-out by topic; EventBridge routes events by content rules and takes SaaS and AWS service events.
pairs.pick_a: High-throughput fan-out to many subscribers with simple filtering.
pairs.pick_b: Event-driven integration where rules match on event fields, schedules, or partner SaaS sources.

pairs.tell: Streams is a log you write consumers for; Firehose is a managed pipe that delivers to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with no consumer code.
pairs.pick_a: Custom real-time processing, multiple consumers, or replay.
pairs.pick_b: Just land the data in a destination, with optional buffering and transformation.

pairs.tell: Kinesis is AWS-native and simple to run; MSK is managed Apache Kafka for teams that already speak Kafka.
pairs.pick_a: New streaming workloads that want the least operations work.
pairs.pick_b: Existing Kafka producers, consumers, and tooling you want to keep.

pairs.tell: Step Functions orchestrates a multi-step workflow with state; SQS only decouples one producer from one consumer stage.
pairs.pick_a: Ordered steps with branching, retries, timeouts, and a human approval wait.
pairs.pick_b: A single hand-off that absorbs bursts between two components.

pairs.tell: A security group is stateful, allow-only, on the instance; a NACL is stateless, allow and deny, on the subnet.
pairs.pick_a: Default control for every resource: allow the app tier to reach the database port.
pairs.pick_b: A coarse subnet-wide deny, such as blocking a known bad address range. Remember return traffic rules.

pairs.tell: Peering is a one-to-one link that is not transitive; Transit Gateway is a hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks.
pairs.pick_a: Two or three VPCs that need to talk, at the lowest cost.
pairs.pick_b: Dozens of VPCs plus VPN or Direct Connect, with central routing.

pairs.tell: An internet gateway allows traffic in and out for public subnets; a NAT gateway lets private subnets reach out while blocking inbound connections.
pairs.pick_a: Load balancers and bastion-free public endpoints in a public subnet.
pairs.pick_b: Private app servers that must download patches or call external APIs.

pairs.tell: A gateway endpoint is a free route-table entry for S3 and DynamoDB only; an interface endpoint is a PrivateLink network interface for many services, billed per hour.
pairs.pick_a: Private access from a VPC to S3 or DynamoDB without NAT charges.
pairs.pick_b: Private access to other AWS services or to a partner service exposed through PrivateLink.

pairs.tell: Direct Connect is a dedicated private line with steady latency but is not encrypted by default; VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the internet that you can set up in minutes.
pairs.pick_a: Large, steady hybrid traffic with predictable latency; add MACsec or a VPN over it for encryption.
pairs.pick_b: Fast, cheap, encrypted connectivity, or as a backup path for Direct Connect.

pairs.tell: ALB works at layer 7 and routes by path or host; NLB works at layer 4 with static IPs and very high throughput.
pairs.pick_a: HTTP and HTTPS apps, microservices behind one endpoint, path-based routing.
pairs.pick_b: TCP or UDP traffic, static IPs for allow-lists, or millions of connections per second.

pairs.tell: CloudFront caches HTTP content at the edge; Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs and routes TCP or UDP over the AWS backbone without caching.
pairs.pick_a: Websites, APIs, and media that benefit from caching near users.
pairs.pick_b: Non-HTTP traffic, gaming, or fast regional failover behind fixed IPs.

pairs.tell: Latency routing sends users to the Region that answers fastest; geolocation routing sends users by where they are, regardless of speed.
pairs.pick_a: Global performance across several Regions.
pairs.pick_b: Data residency, language, or licensing rules tied to a country.

pairs.tell: A Region is a geographic area; an AZ is an isolated data center group inside it. Multi-AZ is for high availability, multi-Region is for disaster recovery.
pairs.pick_a: Choose by user latency, data residency, service availability, and price.
pairs.pick_b: Spread every production tier across at least two AZs.

pairs.tell: EBS is a block disk in one AZ, usually attached to one instance; EFS is a shared NFS file system many instances mount across AZs.
pairs.pick_a: A database or boot volume that needs low-latency block storage.
pairs.pick_b: Shared files for a fleet of Linux instances or containers.

pairs.tell: EFS is a mounted file system with directories and file locks; S3 is object storage you reach over an API, with virtually unlimited scale.
pairs.pick_a: Applications that expect a POSIX file path.
pairs.pick_b: Data lakes, backups, static assets, and anything accessed by key over HTTP.

pairs.tell: Both return data in milliseconds; Standard-IA suits data read about monthly, Glacier Instant Retrieval suits data read about quarterly at lower storage cost and higher retrieval cost.
pairs.pick_a: Backups or older files you still open now and then.
pairs.pick_b: Archives like medical images that are rarely read but must open immediately.

pairs.tell: Storage Gateway gives on-premises apps ongoing access to cloud storage; DataSync moves data from one place to another as a transfer job.
pairs.pick_a: Hybrid file shares or backups that keep running on premises.
pairs.pick_b: One-time or scheduled migration of large file sets into S3, EFS, or FSx.

pairs.tell: DataSync copies files and objects; DMS migrates and replicates databases, including ongoing change data capture.
pairs.pick_a: NFS or SMB shares and object stores.
pairs.pick_b: Moving an Oracle or SQL Server database to RDS or Aurora with minimal downtime.

pairs.tell: Multi-AZ is a synchronous standby for failover that does not serve reads (for a Multi-AZ DB instance); a read replica is an asynchronous copy that serves reads.
pairs.pick_a: High availability: survive an AZ or instance failure.
pairs.pick_b: Scale read traffic or run reporting queries away from the primary.

pairs.tell: RDS runs standard engines on attached storage; Aurora is AWS-built MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible storage replicated six ways across three AZs.
pairs.pick_a: Small or steady databases, or engines Aurora does not offer, like Oracle and SQL Server.
pairs.pick_b: Higher throughput, faster failover, up to 15 readers, or Global Database.

pairs.tell: RDS is relational with joins and flexible queries; DynamoDB is key-value at any scale, but you must design the access patterns first.
pairs.pick_a: Orders, ledgers, and reporting with joins and ad hoc queries.
pairs.pick_b: Known key lookups at very high scale with single-digit millisecond latency.

pairs.tell: ElastiCache is a cache in front of a database; MemoryDB is a durable in-memory primary database with a multi-AZ transaction log.
pairs.pick_a: Cut read latency and database load; losing the cache is acceptable.
pairs.pick_b: You need Redis-compatible speed and cannot lose writes.

pairs.tell: Redshift is a data warehouse you load and tune for heavy repeated queries; Athena is serverless SQL over files in S3, billed per data scanned.
pairs.pick_a: Dashboards and BI with many concurrent, complex queries every day.
pairs.pick_b: Ad hoc or occasional queries on a data lake with no cluster to run.

pairs.tell: Glue is serverless ETL with a data catalog; EMR is a managed Spark and Hadoop cluster you size and tune.
pairs.pick_a: Scheduled ETL jobs and a catalog without managing clusters.
pairs.pick_b: Large or long-running Spark workloads that need custom tuning or frameworks.

pairs.tell: EC2 is a server you run and patch; Lambda runs your function per event for up to 15 minutes and bills per invocation.
pairs.pick_a: Steady load, long processes, OS control, or special hardware.
pairs.pick_b: Spiky, event-driven, short tasks where idle time should cost nothing.

pairs.tell: ECS is AWS-native container orchestration with less to learn; EKS is managed Kubernetes with its ecosystem and portability.
pairs.pick_a: A team that wants containers on AWS with the least operational overhead.
pairs.pick_b: A team already on Kubernetes, or one that needs Helm charts, operators, or multi-cloud portability.

pairs.tell: Fargate runs containers with no nodes to manage; the EC2 launch type runs them on instances you size and patch.
pairs.pick_a: Variable workloads where you want to pay per task and skip node management.
pairs.pick_b: Steady, large fleets where reserved or Spot instances lower cost, or GPU needs.

pairs.tell: Lambda is per event with a 15 minute limit; Fargate runs a container as long as you need.
pairs.pick_a: Short event handlers and glue code.
pairs.pick_b: Long-running services, large dependencies, or jobs that exceed 15 minutes.

pairs.tell: Savings Plans trade a 1 or 3 year commitment for a discount on steady usage; Spot uses spare capacity at a deep discount but can be reclaimed with a 2 minute notice.
pairs.pick_a: The always-on baseline of your fleet.
pairs.pick_b: Fault-tolerant batch, CI, or stateless workers that can be interrupted.

pairs.tell: CloudFormation is declarative YAML or JSON templates; CDK lets you write infrastructure in a programming language and synthesizes CloudFormation.
pairs.pick_a: Teams that want plain templates reviewed as data.
pairs.pick_b: Teams that want loops, types, and reusable constructs in TypeScript or Python.

pairs.tell: CloudTrail records who called which API; CloudWatch records how the system is performing with metrics, logs, and alarms.
pairs.pick_a: Audits and investigations: who deleted the bucket?
pairs.pick_b: Operations: is latency up, and should someone be paged?

pairs.tell: CloudTrail answers who did it; Config answers what the resource looks like now, how it changed, and whether it complies with a rule.
pairs.pick_a: API activity history for security review.
pairs.pick_b: Compliance rules such as every S3 bucket must block public access.

pairs.tell: KMS manages encryption keys and never hands out the key material; Secrets Manager stores secret values such as database passwords and can rotate them.
pairs.pick_a: Encrypt data at rest in S3, EBS, or RDS.
pairs.pick_b: Store and rotate credentials an application reads at runtime.

pairs.tell: Secrets Manager adds built-in rotation and cross-account sharing at a per-secret cost; Parameter Store is cheaper configuration storage with optional encrypted values.
pairs.pick_a: Database credentials that must rotate automatically.
pairs.pick_b: Feature flags, endpoints, and settings, including some encrypted values.

pairs.tell: A role gives temporary credentials to whoever is allowed to assume it; a user has long-lived credentials tied to one identity.
pairs.pick_a: Every workload on AWS, and human access through SSO.
pairs.pick_b: Rare cases that truly need long-lived keys; prefer roles and Identity Center instead.

pairs.tell: An IAM policy grants permissions to a principal; an SCP sets the maximum permissions for accounts in an organization and grants nothing by itself.
pairs.pick_a: Give a role exactly the actions it needs.
pairs.pick_b: Guardrails such as no account may leave approved Regions or disable CloudTrail.

pairs.tell: Cognito signs in your application's customers; Identity Center signs your workforce into AWS accounts and business apps.
pairs.pick_a: Sign-up and sign-in for a consumer or partner app.
pairs.pick_b: Employee single sign-on across many AWS accounts.

pairs.tell: WAF filters layer 7 requests by rules such as SQL injection or rate limits; Shield protects against network and transport layer DDoS attacks.
pairs.pick_a: Block bad HTTP requests in front of CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway.
pairs.pick_b: Absorb volumetric DDoS; Shield Standard is on by default, Advanced adds response support.

pairs.tell: GuardDuty detects active threats from logs and network activity; Inspector scans your workloads for known vulnerabilities before they are exploited.
pairs.pick_a: Alert on a compromised instance talking to a known bad host.
pairs.pick_b: Find unpatched packages in EC2, container images, and Lambda.

pairs.tell: Bedrock is an API to existing foundation models; SageMaker AI is where you build, train, and host your own models.
pairs.pick_a: Generative AI features using Claude or other foundation models without managing infrastructure.
pairs.pick_b: Custom models, full control of training and hosting, or classic ML.

pairs.tell: Knowledge Bases is managed RAG that retrieves chunks and feeds them to a model; Kendra is an enterprise search engine that returns ranked documents and answers.
pairs.pick_a: A chatbot that answers questions grounded in your documents.
pairs.pick_b: Search across many enterprise connectors, sometimes used as the retriever for RAG.

pairs.tell: Guardrails filter what a model says; they do not decide which documents a user may see. Enforce that with identity and metadata filters on retrieval.
pairs.pick_a: Block harmful topics, redact PII in responses, and check grounding.
pairs.pick_b: Make sure a user only retrieves documents they are entitled to.

pairs.tell: High availability keeps a service running through component failures; disaster recovery restores it after a larger event, measured by RPO and RTO.
pairs.pick_a: Multi-AZ deployments, health checks, and automatic failover.
pairs.pick_b: Backups and a second Region, with tested restore and failover runbooks.

pairs.tell: RPO is how much data you can lose, measured in time; RTO is how long you can be down.
pairs.pick_a: Drives backup frequency and replication choice.
pairs.pick_b: Drives how much infrastructure you keep warm in the recovery Region.

pairs.tell: Pilot light keeps only the core data replicated and scales everything else up on failover; warm standby runs a smaller full copy that is already serving.
pairs.pick_a: RTO of tens of minutes to hours at low cost.
pairs.pick_b: RTO of minutes, paying for a scaled-down live environment.

pairs.tell: Replication copies mistakes instantly; backups and versioning let you go back to a point before the mistake.
pairs.pick_a: Recover from deletion, corruption, or ransomware.
pairs.pick_b: Survive infrastructure failure with an up-to-date copy.
